CKB Escrow Security Test Kit A Reusable Rust Testing Framework and Reference Implementation for CKB Escrow Scripts

Applicant: Zuhudev and Charles
Funding Requested: $2,000 USDI
Estimated Duration: 8 Weeks
Target Network: CKB Testnet
Project Type: Open-source developer infrastructure and smart-contract security tooling

  1. Project Summary

CKB Escrow Security Test Kit is an open-source developer resource designed to help CKB developers identify and prevent common transaction-level vulnerabilities in escrow scripts.

The project will deliver a reusable Rust-based security test suite, a minimal reference escrow implementation, and documented adversarial transaction examples. Developers will be able to use the test kit to examine whether escrow logic correctly enforces authorization, fund accounting, state transitions, recipient restrictions, and timeout conditions.

The project is not intended to introduce another escrow application or compete with existing CKB products. It will provide a technical testing resource that can complement existing and future escrow implementations.

The initial implementation will focus on native CKB capacity and milestone-based escrow conditions. It will be a testnet and development tool, not a production-ready financial product or security audit.

  1. Problem Statement

Escrow applications depend on transaction validation rules that must remain correct even when users construct unexpected or malicious transactions.

A script may appear to work under normal conditions but still contain weaknesses involving unauthorized releases, invalid state transitions, recipient redirection, repeated settlement attempts, or incorrect accounting across multiple cells.

These risks are particularly important in CKB because applications rely on transaction-level script validation and cell state transitions. Security assumptions must therefore be tested against complete transaction structures, not only isolated application functions.

There is already meaningful escrow-related development within the CKB ecosystem. PactAgent has explored milestone-based agreements, proof submission, approval, refunds, disputes, and reusable escrow infrastructure. Other escrow application work has also been shared with the community.

This proposal does not assume that these projects are insecure or that the ecosystem lacks escrow implementations.

Instead, it addresses a narrower developer tooling opportunity: providing a documented, reproducible set of adversarial transaction tests and reference security invariants that escrow developers can adapt when testing their own implementations.

The need for escrow-related safeguards is also reflected in previous CKB community discussions about milestone-based fund disbursement and the risks associated with upfront payments and fund recovery.

References:

Nervos DAO post-payment and escrow discussion: [DIS] DAO资金发放改为”后付费“ | Transition to ”Post-Payment“ Model for DAO Fund Disbursement PactAgent infrastructure development: PactAgent: From Application to Infrastructure CKB Escrow application discussion: CKB Escrow: a decentralized escrow app for goods and services on Nervos CKB CKB Rust development and testing documentation: Rust Script Quick Start | Nervos CKB 3. Proposed Solution

We will build a focused security-testing kit consisting of three connected components.

A. Reusable Rust Security Test Suite

A collection of transaction-level test fixtures designed to examine common escrow security properties.

The initial test categories will include:

Unauthorized release: Verify that an escrow cannot be released without the required authorization. Double release and replay: Verify that a completed milestone or escrow cannot be settled more than once. State integrity: Verify that milestone states cannot be reset, skipped, or changed through invalid transitions. Recipient integrity: Verify that funds cannot be redirected to an unauthorized recipient. Timeout enforcement: Verify that refunds are permitted only under the defined timeout conditions and that premature refunds are rejected. Transaction isolation and accounting: Verify that multiple escrow cells, unrelated transaction inputs, and outputs cannot be used to bypass escrow-specific accounting rules.

The tests will construct complete CKB transactions and verify their execution using the established CKB testing workflow.

B. Minimal Rust Reference Escrow Script

We will implement a small reference escrow script to demonstrate the security rules being tested.

The reference implementation will support:

Escrow creation with defined participants and conditions. Authorized milestone release. State transition validation. Timeout-based refunds. Native CKB capacity accounting. Validation of relevant transaction inputs and outputs.

The implementation will deliberately remain limited. It will not include a marketplace, dispute-resolution interface, multisignature system, governance module, or production fund-management service.

A deliberately vulnerable reference variant will also be included for selected test cases. This will demonstrate that the attack scenarios are meaningful: the vulnerable implementation should accept the relevant attack, while the protected implementation should reject it.

C. Developer Documentation and Integration Examples

We will provide practical documentation explaining:

How the test suite is structured. How to run the tests locally. How to add a new adversarial transaction scenario. How the reference escrow script enforces its security conditions. How developers can adapt the test patterns to their own escrow scripts. How to reproduce the testnet demonstration.

Where useful, we will include a minimal TypeScript example showing how a developer application can prepare and interact with the reference escrow workflow using CKB development tooling.

The documentation will distinguish between properties demonstrated by the reference implementation and properties that must be independently verified in an external project.

  1. Technical Design

The initial reference implementation will use a defined set of escrow participants, release conditions, and timeout rules.

Lock arguments: Store or commit to the authorization identity, refund recipient, timeout configuration, and escrow configuration reference.

Cell data: Represent the escrow’s current state and milestone information. Native CKB capacity will represent the locked value.

Release validation: Require the specified authorization and a valid state transition. Validate the relevant transaction structure and destination conditions.

Refund validation: Permit the designated refund path only after the configured timeout condition has been satisfied.

The exact serialization format, state representation, transaction invariants, and use of CKB since will be specified during the first development phase.

The implementation will not assume that a script can control every aspect of an application-level agreement. The test suite will clearly identify which guarantees are enforced on-chain and which remain application responsibilities.

  1. Deliverables

At completion, the project will publish:

An open-source Rust security-testing repository. A minimal CKB reference escrow script. A deliberately vulnerable reference variant for selected attack demonstrations. At least six documented adversarial test categories with reproducible transaction fixtures. Positive test cases demonstrating legitimate escrow creation, release, and refund. Documentation explaining the security invariants and how to extend the test suite. A CKB Testnet demonstration with transaction hashes. A final technical report containing test results, known limitations, and instructions for independent verification.

All source code, test cases, and documentation produced through the grant will be publicly accessible.

  1. Security Validation and Acceptance Criteria

The project will be considered complete when the following conditions are met:

The Rust reference script builds successfully. The security test suite executes through the documented CKB testing workflow. Each of the six attack categories has a reproducible transaction-level test. Selected attacks succeed against the deliberately vulnerable reference variant and are rejected by the protected implementation. Legitimate escrow creation, milestone release, and timeout refund transactions pass. Tests cover multiple escrow cells and transactions containing unrelated inputs and outputs. The test suite documents the expected result and security property for every scenario. The reference implementation is demonstrated on CKB Testnet. Testnet transaction hashes, source code, setup instructions, and execution results are published. At least one independent developer review or fresh-environment reproduction is documented, subject to reviewer availability.

Passing these tests will demonstrate the behavior of the reference implementation. It will not constitute a formal security audit or guarantee that every external escrow implementation is secure.

  1. Eight-Week Development Timeline Week Activities Expected Output 1 Review existing CKB escrow implementations, document the project boundary, define threat model and security invariants. Gap analysis and security specification 2 Design the Rust test architecture, transaction fixtures, and attack scenarios. Test architecture and initial fixtures 3 Implement the minimal Rust reference escrow script and creation flow. Working reference script 4 Implement authorization, milestone release, state validation, and timeout logic. Core escrow functionality 5 Build vulnerable reference cases and adversarial transaction fixtures. Reproducible attack scenarios 6 Complete the six security test categories, run tests, and resolve identified defects. Security test suite 7 Prepare developer documentation and minimal integration examples. Documentation and examples 8 Deploy the reference demonstration on CKB Testnet, publish results, seek independent reproduction, and submit the final report. Public release and completion report 8. Budget Breakdown

Total requested: $2,000 USDI

Workstream Allocation Existing implementation review, threat model, and security specification $250 Rust reference escrow implementation $550 Adversarial transaction testing framework and fixtures $650 Documentation and integration examples $250 Testnet demonstration, independent reproduction support, and final report $300 Total $2,000

The budget is tied to the delivery of the specified technical outputs. It does not include a production security audit, ongoing maintenance, or deployment of a public escrow service.

  1. Team Zuhudev — Full-stack Blockchain Developer

Responsible for the core implementation, blockchain development, developer tooling, and integration work.

GitHub: https://github.com/zuhudev
Telegram: @zuhudevram
Email: robinsonnos@gmail.com

Charles — Full-stack Developer

Responsible for supporting implementation, application integration, testing workflows, and developer documentation.

GitHub: charleslukes (Charles Chiakwa) · GitHub

The team will divide implementation and testing responsibilities and document individual contributions throughout the project.

  1. Previous CKB Ecosystem Contribution

CKB Builder Lab is an existing developer learning and experimentation platform created to help developers understand CKB concepts through guided learning paths, browser simulations, and practical challenges.

Repository: GitHub - devnash11/ckb-builder-lab · GitHub
Live platform: https://ckb-builder-lab.vercel.app

The proposed Security Test Kit addresses a different technical layer.

CKB Builder Lab focuses on developer learning and experimentation, while this project focuses on transaction-level security testing and reusable Rust development resources.

Together, these resources can support developers at different stages of building on CKB.

  1. Ecosystem Impact

The project will contribute to the CKB ecosystem in four ways.

Improved developer security practices: Developers will have concrete adversarial examples for testing escrow-related transaction logic rather than relying exclusively on successful-path demonstrations.

Reusable open-source infrastructure: The test fixtures, reference implementation, and documentation can be adapted by other developers working on CKB applications.

Stronger technical education: The project will turn common escrow security assumptions into practical examples that developers can inspect, execute, and extend.

Complementary ecosystem development: Rather than introducing another end-user escrow product, the project will provide testing resources that can complement existing applications and infrastructure.

We will measure the initial impact through repository publication, test coverage across the six attack categories, reproducible execution instructions, testnet evidence, and documented developer feedback.

  1. Risks and Limitations

The project will maintain a deliberately narrow scope to ensure delivery within eight weeks.

The test kit will initially focus on native CKB capacity, not sUDT or arbitrary token standards. It will not claim compatibility with every existing escrow implementation. External projects will not be described as insecure without permission and independent evidence. The reference script will not be marketed as production-ready. No formal audit, mainnet deployment, dispute arbitration service, or long-term maintenance commitment is included. Any security property that cannot be enforced directly by the script will be documented as an application-level responsibility. 13. Project Completion and Public Reporting

At the end of the eight-week period, we will publish the repository, implementation documentation, test results, testnet transaction references, and final technical report.

The completion report will include:

What was delivered. Which security scenarios were tested. Results from the vulnerable and protected reference implementations. Reproducible commands and environment requirements. Known limitations and future improvements. Feedback received from independent developers.

The work will be publicly available so that CKB developers can inspect, reproduce, and build upon it.

  1. Final Request

We are requesting $2,000 USDI to complete an eight-week open-source development project focused on improving the security-testing resources available to CKB developers.

The objective is not to build another escrow interface. It is to deliver practical, reusable security tests and a reference implementation that make it easier to identify weaknesses in CKB escrow transaction logic before applications are deployed.

By publishing the code, adversarial test cases, and reproducible examples, this project will contribute a focused developer resource to the Nervos ecosystem.

posts.cooked:
Good scope: testing the transaction shape, not only the happy path. Your first phase leaves the since usage and serialization open, so here are five CKB-specific decisions I would settle in the week-1 spec, because each one changes what the tests have to check. I read the proposal and the CKB RFCs, then ran points 1 and 4 on a local CKB dev chain (ckb 0.210.0), and points 3 and 5 and the group case on a deliberately simple toy lock script of mine in ckb-testtool (so “naive” below means my toy, not your design). Point 2 is a design decision and was not run. Happy to share the scripts.

  1. Relative timeouts restart on every milestone. A relative since is measured from the block that committed the transaction that created the input cell. If each release re-creates the escrow cell with the remainder, the refund clock restarts every time. On the dev chain, a relative since of 15 blocks was rejected right after creation (Immature), accepted after 15 blocks, and the re-created cell was rejected again right away with the same since. An absolute deadline did not restart: the re-created cell was spendable immediately after the deadline. Decide between an absolute deadline and restart-on-purpose, and test both.

  2. After the timeout, is release still valid? Both paths spend the same cell, so after the deadline a refund and a late release are competing transactions, and ordering decides the outcome, not the contract’s intent. If release stays valid, a refund can be front-run by a late release, and the other way round. Pick one rule and test the race.

  3. Fees on permissionless paths. Fee is inputs minus outputs and goes to the miner. On an authorized path the sender only burns their own funds, but if anyone can trigger the refund after the timeout, a transaction with outputs below the escrowed capacity lets a third party burn it (the difference goes to the miner). In my toy lock, a refund paying 400 of 1000 was accepted by the naive check and rejected once the lock required outputs of at least the escrowed capacity. Require that, and fees from another input.

  4. Minimum capacity breaks small milestones. Every output must hold at least its occupied capacity (61 CKB for a plain secp256k1 lock cell with no data; yours will differ with args and data). On the dev chain a 60.99999999 CKB output was rejected (InsufficientCellCapacity), 61 was accepted, and a 1000 CKB cell could not be split 950/50 or 970/30 because the remainder cell was below the minimum. Any milestone that would leave a remainder below that minimum cannot be released, so the funds sit until the refund path. Worth a fixture, and a note in the docs.

  5. Terms are not checked at creation. A lock only runs when its cell is spent, so anyone can create a cell with your lock args and any terms, for example a timeout of zero. In my toy test a cell with the escrow lock, deadline 0 and “approved” state was created from an unrelated cell’s input and accepted. To the seller it looks like a real escrow. A type script (with a unique id) can enforce well-formed terms at creation; either way the docs should say that the counterparty must check the args against what was agreed.

On the group case in “transaction isolation”: a lock group contains only input cells and runs once per transaction, so release logic must count its group inputs and bind exactly one continuation output through Source::Output. With two escrow cells in one transaction where only one was approved, the naive lock (which looked at the first cell only) accepted it and the hardened lock rejected it.

One suggestion on acceptance: make the independent reproduction a milestone gate, not “subject to reviewer availability”.

Sources: RFC 0017 (tx valid since), RFC 0022 (transaction structure).

Hi @devnash, this is a really useful kit. Timeout and refund paths are exactly where escrow scripts tend to break.

I’m the author of CSR (CKB Service Runner), and there’s one application-level gap I’d suggest documenting: the script can permit a refund once the timeout has passed, but someone still has to submit that refund transaction. Today that’s usually the user or the project’s own server.

With CSR, the escrow creator (or the app) posts a job cell with an at block or at time trigger that matches the refund timeout. The runner proves the trigger through the since field, reads the escrow cell through a chain-read host call, and returns the refund transaction skeleton to the refund recipient committed in the lock args. A “when cell X is spent” condition can cancel the job if the escrow is released first.

That could also make a nice extra test case: refund liveness with no trusted server.

Status, honestly: CSR’s runtime and contracts are testnet only, and mainnet paid services are gated until the runner set is large and diverse enough. An October audit found no critical issues, and fixes are underway. If you’d like a testnet job pointed at your reference escrow, I’m glad to help.

posts.cooked:
Hi @devnash,

Thank you for your continued interest in the Spark Program and for submitting the CKB Escrow Security Test Kit proposal.

After review by the Spark Program committee, your proposal’s status is Pending. This is not a rejection, but an invitation to revise your proposal.

The committee recognizes the value of the project concept: a reusable security testing framework for CKB escrow scripts could make a meaningful contribution to developers’ security practices.

Generality and Ease of Use Across a Broader Ecosystem: Consistent with the ckb-adversary proposal, which is also a security tool, the committee is interested in two questions. How does the ckb-escrow-security-test-kit achieve greater generality so that other projects can use it for security scans? And what technical approaches enable it to cover more general use cases, allowing more applications and smart contracts to use the tool?

Please revise and resubmit your proposal based on this feedback. We’ll arrange another review as soon as possible.

Best regards
xingtian
On behalf of the Spark Program Committee

Hi @xingtianchunyan,

How the kit achieves generality. Three layers; only the middle one is per project.

  1. Generic mutation engine. Starts from any transaction the target script accepts and changes Cell Model fields every script sees: output capacity, lock args or type; extra inputs or outputs; cell deps and dep groups; header deps; since (absolute or relative, and its metric); hash_type; witness bytes; occupied capacity; fee. Nothing depends on the source language or on escrow logic.

  2. Small target descriptor. A TOML/JSON file declaring where the semantics live: which lock args hold participants, refund recipient and deadline; the cell-data layout; legal transitions; and invariants such as authorization, conservation, one continuation output per group input, and monotonic state. Without one, the structural mutations still run and are reported as review, not findings.

  3. Invariant oracle. Built-in CKB invariants (capacity conservation, occupied capacity floor, since maturity, dep-group resolution, Source::Output binding) plus the declared ones. A mutant becomes a finding only when the script accepts it and the oracle shows value or authority moving to a party that should not get it.

The harness runs the compiled script through the standard CKB testing workflow and reasons per lock group and per type group, so it needs no source and works on scripts we did not write.

How it covers more than escrow. The six escrow categories are instances of four generic families: unauthorized spend, replay or double-settle, state-transition violation, and accounting or isolation violation. Any stateful cell script with a continuation output maps onto them — vesting and treasury locks, milestone grants, payment-channel or Fiber funding locks, subscription cells, restricted-transfer xUDT. The revision will demonstrate this with two adapters (the escrow reference and one non-escrow lock) and one third-party port, rather than assert it.

Limits. A signature lock refuses every mutation unless a signing hook is supplied; scripts that verify proofs or read external state need a statement-rebuild hook; one transaction is one code path; off-chain terms and who submits a refund remain application responsibilities.

Thank you for taking the time to revise the proposal based on our earlier feedback.

The committee has completed its review and has determined that the proposal does not fall within the scope of the Spark Program. Therefore, we regret to inform you that the proposal has been rejected.
